title: Managing Multiple Company Codes with SAP Document AI
author: tobias_weller
text:
Managing Multiple Company Codes with SAP Document AI 
 Large enterprises rarely process documents in a single legal entity. Accounts payable teams handle supplier invoices across dozens of company codes. HR shared services process onboarding documents for employees across multiple subsidiaries. Quality management teams receive certificates and inspection reports addressed to different plants. Procurement teams handle order confirmations sent to different buying entities. 
 In all of these scenarios, the same challenge comes up early: how do you configure SAP Document AI to handle multiple company codes or legal entities cleanly? The document type is the same across entities. The fields you want to extract are the same. But the legal entity matters for routing, authorization, and downstream ERP posting. 
 This post walks through a clean architecture for managing multiple company codes in SAP Document AI, and then goes further by using the workflow engine to inject organizational context that the document itself cannot provide.

title: Stay Current with SAP SuccessFactors Talent Intelligence Hub: 2H 2026 Updates
author: jahnavia
text:
Hello SAP SuccessFactors Community! 
 The 2H 2026 release is here, bringing 14 updates to Talent Intelligence Hub, from new Growth Portfolio capabilities and certificate management to skills governance, data sources and two key deprecations. Let's walk through what has changed. 
 Talent Intelligence Hub 
 1. Minor Visual Changes in 2H 2026 
 Two text changes are worth noting: 
 Certificates in the Growth Portfolio that are awaiting reviewer approval and not yet added now show a Validity Status of Not Applicable instead of Not Yet Active. 

 On the Manage Data Sources page, partner data sources are now added to the main page with the Add from list button instead of Add. 

 2. New To-Do Categories for Growth Portfolio Cards on the Home Page 
 Two new To-Do categories now appear on the Home page for Growth Portfolio tasks: 
 Proficiency Level Change Requests: shown when an employee changes a proficiency level on an attribute that has an approval workflow. The card shows the employee, attribute type, requested level and previous level. 

 Certificate Change Requests: the card shows the employee, certificate name, issue date and submission date. 

 SAP recommends completing all pending To-Do tasks before using the new categories, as older tasks may show actions that are no longer applicable. 
 3. REST API for Growth Portfolio Export 
 A new REST API exports employee skills data from the Growth Portfolio for reporting, analysis and other downstream uses, complementing the export options in Integration Center. 
 Included: active and inactive skill records for active and inactive users, and current proficiency levels. 
 Not included: recommended skills not yet added, and historical proficiency levels. 
 Only authorized users and partner data sources can access the data through this API. 
 4. New Sorting and Filtering Option to Export Attributes 
 The updated Talent Intelligence Hub Attribute Export Integration Center Definition (.icd) file from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub adds advanced filtering and sorting. For example, you can export skills and exclude competencies, and order the output as you prefer. Time-based filters are not supported yet and do not affect results. SAP recommends moving to the updated file, as the existing template will no longer be supported from 1H 2027. 

 5. Enhancements to Skills Governance and Standardization 
 Skills in the Attributes Library, including those pending administrator review on the Skills Governance page, are now automatically scanned and mapped to their SAP Taxonomy names. 
 Skills landing page: Taxonomy Mapping and SAP Taxonomy Name replace Standardization Status as filters and columns, and the Skills Governance button shows the count of skills awaiting review. 

 Creating a skill: the Proposed Name and Standardization Status fields become SAP Taxonomy Name and Taxonomy Mapping. The options are Taxonomy name and mapping (renamed to the SAP name, included in AI recommendations, translations inherited), Entered name and mapping (keeps your name, included in AI recommendations, translations maintained manually) and No mapping (custom skill, excluded from AI recommendations, translations maintained manually). 

 Publishing from the Imported tab: Taxonomy Mapping is now chosen per skill in the Publish dialog, and each option shows the resulting skill name. 
 Inferred Skills tab: a new Inference Details tab shows the inferred count and confidence score for a skill. 

 6. Employee Defined Validity for Certificates 
 Certificates can now be set to User Defined validity. The system then stops calculating the expiry date from the issue date and duration, and employees pick the Expiry Date themselves with a date picker when adding the certificate to their Growth Portfolio. That date drives expiry notifications and expiring soon indicators, which suits certificates with non-standard validity periods. 

 7. Enhancements to Data Sources 
 Besides partner integrations, custom data sources can now be created on the Manage Data Sources page with a name, code and optional description. The code is automatically prefixed with CUST_, and the source is Inactive until activated. 
 Rating Overwrite Allowed and Rating Lowering Allowed default to No for custom data sources. 
 Trusted Data Source defaults to No, so skills governance applies. Setting it to Yes bypasses governance. 
 When skills from a custom data source are imported, its name appears in the skill's Timeline. 

 8. Deprecation of Center of Capabilities 
 Center of Capabilities reaches End of Development and End of Maintenance on November 13, 2026, and will be deleted on May 12, 2028. SAP recommends migrating to Talent Intelligence Hub by 2H 2027 to manage competency data. 
 Action: Required. Future dates are subject to change. 
 9. New Archive Option for Skills in Growth Portfolio 
 Employees can archive non-role-based skills that no longer match their role or development goals, without permanently removing them. Archived skills move to a separate Archived tab and are excluded from active learning recommendations and opportunities, but stay available in historical searches for succession and recruiting. They can be reactivated or removed, and activity recorded from other sources does not change them. Archiving applies only to skills, not other attribute types. 

 10. Enhanced Flow for Removal of Attributes in Growth Portfolio 
 Attributes an employee removes now move to an Inactive tab for their attribute type. They are read-only, and their opportunity recommendations and development goals are no longer shown. Certificates do not support Remove yet. 
 An employee can add an inactive attribute back from its details page or the attribute picker. 

 Completing a linked activity elsewhere, such as an Opportunity Marketplace assignment or a Learning course, reactivates it automatically. 
 If an administrator sets the attribute to inactive in Talent Intelligence Hub, it disappears from the tab and returns once reactivated. The Timeline logs inactivation and reactivation as separate entries. 
 11. Enhancements to Certificates in Growth Portfolio 
 Several changes simplify certificate management: 
 Acquired tab: certificates the employee has added, split into Critical for Role, Non-Critical for Role and Others (added independently, not tied to the role). 

 Missing tab: role-related certificates not yet added, split into Critical for Role and Non-Critical for Role. 
 Withdraw: employees can withdraw a certificate that is pending reviewer approval or sent back for corrections. 

 Action Required filter: shows certificates to Renew , Resubmit (sent back by reviewers) or Add Critical (critical for the role, not yet added). 

 12. Role-Based Skill Classification in Job Profile 
 A new Requirement Level field on the Manage Job Profile Content page marks each skill mapped to a job role as Mandatory (core to the role) or Optional (relevant but not strictly required). Employees in the role then see these skills in their Growth Portfolio tagged as Critical for Role or Non-Critical for Role, helping them tell essential skills from complementary ones. 

 13. Support for Mapping Certificates with Job Roles 
 A new Mapped Certificates tab on the Manage Job Profile Content page lets administrators map Talent Intelligence Hub certificates to job roles in Job Profile Builder. The Critical toggle marks a certificate as essential for the role. Mapped certificates appear for employees in the role under Missing, as Critical for Role or Non-Critical for Role, and can be added directly from there. 

 14. Deprecation of Job Description Manager 
 Job Description Manager, the framework for managing legacy job families and roles, reached End of Development and End of Maintenance on May 15, 2026, and will be deleted on November 12, 2027. SAP recommends moving to Job Profile Builder and Talent Intelligence Hub to manage job families, job roles, skills and other attributes. 
 Action: Required. Future dates are subject to change. 
 That wraps up the 2H 2026 Talent Intelligence Hub updates. Do refer to the SAP Help Portal and What's New Viewer for the latest details, and let me know in the comments which update you are most looking forward to.

title: The Hidden Security Habit Every SAP BTP Admin Must Master: Service Key Rotation
author: Yogananda
text:
Introduction: the credential nobody owns 
 A service key is usually created in thirty seconds, pasted into a .env file or a CI variable or Destination or any 3rd Party applications, and then forgotten for years. That is exactly why it becomes one of the most dangerous objects in your SAP BTP landscape. 
 If you integrate anything with BTP from outside the platform (a local development machine, an on-premise system, a GitHub Actions pipeline, a low-code tool such as n8n), you almost certainly rely on service keys. They give you a client ID and secret, or a certificate, that unlocks a service instance: XSUAA, Destination, Object Store, Cloud Logging, SAP AI Core and many more. 
 This blogpost explains what service keys really are, why you must rotate them, and how to do it without downtime, using the cf CLI, the btp CLI and a small automation pattern you can drop into a pipeline. 
 What a service key is (and is not) 
 A service key is a set of credentials generated on demand for an existing service instance. It is meant for clients that live outside the platform. Credentials meant for an application running inside Cloud Foundry or Kyma are called service bindings, and they reach the app through VCAP_SERVICES or a Kubernetes secret. The mechanics are the same, which is why this post applies to both. 
 For an XSUAA instance, a key typically contains the following fields: 
 clientid and clientsecret : the OAuth 2.0 client credentials 
 url and uaadomain : the token endpoint host 
 xsappname , identityzone , tenantid : identifiers of the application and subaccount 
 verificationkey : the public key used to validate issued JWTs 
 Whoever holds the clientid and clientsecret can request tokens with the scopes of the service instance, from anywhere on the internet. There is no IP restriction and no user attached. The key is the identity. 
 Credential types 
 Many BTP services let you choose how a key authenticates. The choice decides how painful rotation will be. 

 Credential type 
 What you get 
 Rotation effort 
 Typical risk 

 Client secret (default, binding-secret ) 
 clientid + clientsecret 
 Create a new key, replace the secret everywhere 
 A leaked string works until you delete the key 

 X.509 certificate 
 Client certificate and private key (mTLS) 
 Keys expire by design; re-issue before expiry 
 Needs the private key, not just a string 

 Instance secret 
 One secret shared by the instance 
 Rotation touches every consumer at once 
 Large blast radius 
 For X.509 on XSUAA you request the type when creating the key, with a short validity: 
 cf create-service-key my-xsuaa key-x509 -c '{
 "credential-type": "x509",
 "x509": { "key-length": 2048, "validity": 7, "validity-type": "DAYS" }
}' 
 Supported parameters differ per service, so check the documentation of the service you use on SAP Help Portal . 
 Why rotation is needed 
 A service key never expires on its own (unless you chose X.509 with a validity). Every day it exists, the chance that it has leaked grows, and you never learn about the leak until it is abused. Rotation puts a ceiling on that exposure. 
 Leaks are silent . Keys end up in shell history, screenshots, support tickets, Postman collections, Git commits and CI logs. A leaked key looks identical to a legitimate one in the logs. 
 People and projects leave . The developer who created a key for a proof of concept may have left the company. Rotation, combined with an inventory, forces someone to claim every key or let it die. 
 Blast radius . A key carries the scopes of the whole instance. Short-lived or frequently replaced keys limit how long an attacker can use what they stole. 
 Compliance . Frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and internal security policies commonly require periodic credential rotation and evidence that it happens. 
 Proof that you can do it . The worst time to learn that rotating a credential breaks three undocumented consumers is during an incident. A routine rotation is a fire drill you run on your own schedule. 
 What it buys you in an incident 
 If rotation is a routine, a suspected leak becomes a normal operation: create a new key, move consumers over, delete the old key. If it is not a routine, you face a decision between a possible breach and a possible outage, usually at night. 
 Deleting a key revokes its client secret at the service, so a rotation also invalidates any copy someone made earlier. Tokens that were already issued stay valid until they expire, which is why short token lifetimes matter as well. 
 The zero-downtime pattern: overlap, switch, retire 
 The key point is that a service instance can have several keys at the same time. You never edit a key in place. You add a second one next to the first, and you retire the first only after every consumer has moved. 
 Inventory. List the existing keys and find out who uses each one. 
 Create a new key with a versioned or dated name, for example ci-2026-10 . 
 Distribute the new credentials to your secret store or CI system. 
 Switch the consumers: redeploy, restart or let them reload the secret. 
 Verify that the consumers obtain tokens with the new key and that errors stay flat. 
 Wait a grace period, so that slow consumers (nightly jobs, a colleague's laptop) fail loudly rather than silently. 
 Delete the old key. This is the step that actually closes the leak. 
 Two habits make this reliable. First, name keys with a purpose and a date ( n8n-prod-2026-10 ), so age and owner are visible in a listing. Second, give each consumer its own key. If five systems share one key, you can rotate it only by switching five systems on the same day, and you cannot tell which of them used it last. 
 Hands-on: rotating a key with the CLI 
 Cloud Foundry ( cf CLI) 
 Start with an inventory of the keys on the instance: 
 cf service-keys my-xsuaa 
 Create the replacement key and read its credentials through the API, which is more robust to script than the formatted CLI output: 
 NEW_KEY="n8n-prod-$(date +%Y-%m)"
cf create-service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key my-xsuaa "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq '.credentials' 
 After the consumers have switched and the grace period is over, remove the old key: 
 cf delete-service-key my-xsuaa n8n-prod-2026-09 -f 
 For service bindings used by apps, the equivalent is to create a new binding and restart the app so it reads the new VCAP_SERVICES . A rolling restart avoids downtime: 
 cf restart my-app --strategy rolling 
 Other environments ( btp CLI and Service Manager) 
 In Kyma or any non-Cloud-Foundry environment, keys are called bindings and are managed through Service Manager. The btp CLI exposes them: btp CLI 
 btp list services/binding
btp create services/binding --name ci-2026-10 --service-instance my-xsuaa
btp delete services/binding --name ci-2026-09 --confirm 
 In Kyma, the equivalent is a ServiceBinding resource that writes the credentials to a Kubernetes secret. Creating a second ServiceBinding and pointing the workload at the new secret follows the same overlap pattern. Command flags change between CLI versions, so confirm them with btp help before you script anything. 
 Automating rotation and storing the result 
 Manual rotation works once. A scheduled job works every time. The script below creates a fresh key, hands the credentials to your secret store, and deletes keys older than a grace period. It is a starting point, not a drop-in product: adapt the secret-store call and test it on a non-production instance first. 
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

INSTANCE="$1" # service instance name
PREFIX="$2" # key name prefix, e.g. n8n-prod
GRACE_DAYS="${3:-14}" # how long old keys stay alive

NEW_KEY="${PREFIX}-$(date +%Y%m%d)"
cf create-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY"

GUID=$(cf service-key "$INSTANCE" "$NEW_KEY" --guid)
CREDS=$(cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings/$GUID/details" | jq -c '.credentials')

# 1. Push to your secret store (never echo or log $CREDS)
# e.g. vault kv put secret/btp/$PREFIX value="$CREDS"

# 2. Retire old keys of this prefix beyond the grace period
INST_GUID=$(cf service "$INSTANCE" --guid)
CUTOFF=$(date -u -d "-${GRACE_DAYS} days" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)

cf curl "/v3/service_credential_bindings?type=key&service_instance_guids=${INST_GUID}" \
 | jq -r --arg p "$PREFIX" --arg c "$CUTOFF" --arg n "$NEW_KEY" \
 '.resources[] | select((.name|startswith($p)) and .name != $n and .created_at < $c) | .name' \
 | while read -r OLD; do
 echo "Deleting expired key: $OLD"
 cf delete-service-key "$INSTANCE" "$OLD" -f
 done 
 Where the new credentials should live 
 A dedicated secret manager. HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the SAP Credential Store service on BTP. Consumers fetch the secret at start-up or on a refresh interval, so a rotation needs no redeploy. 
 CI/CD secrets. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI or Jenkins credentials, updated by the rotation job through their API. 
 Not in Git, not in images, not in chat. Not even in a private repository, and not as a plain environment variable baked into a container image. 
 Run the job on a schedule, for example every 60 or 90 days, and make the grace period shorter than the interval. Alert when a rotation fails, because a silent failure is worse than no automation: it creates the false impression that the problem is handled. 
 The cleanest long-term step is to remove the shared secret entirely. Where the service supports it, prefer X.509 credentials with a short validity, or an identity federation flow such as OIDC trust between your CI provider and BTP, so that no long-lived secret exists to rotate. 
 Pitfalls, checklist and conclusion 
 Common pitfalls 
 Deleting before switching. Remove the old key only after you have seen the new one working in production. 
 Forgotten consumers. Cron jobs, notebooks and a colleague's local default-env.json break after the delete. Use the grace period and watch authentication failures. 
 One key for everything. It makes rotation a coordinated big-bang change and hides who uses what. 
 Cached tokens and clients. Applications that read the secret once at start-up need a restart, or a reload mechanism, to pick up the new value. 
 Rotating the key but not the access around it. A new key with the same wide scopes only shortens the exposure. Combine rotation with least-privilege scopes and role collections. 
 No monitoring. Check the audit logs and authentication errors after each rotation; SAP Audit Log service records management operations on service instances. 
 Checklist 
 Every service key has an owner, a purpose and a date in its name 
 One key per consumer, no shared keys 
 Rotation interval defined (for example 90 days) and automated 
 Credentials live in a secret manager, not in code or images 
 Old keys are deleted after a fixed grace period 
 Failures of the rotation job raise an alert 
 Short-lived X.509 or federated identity used wherever the service supports it 
 Conclusion 
 Service key rotation is cheap insurance. It limits how long a leaked credential is useful, it forces you to know who depends on what, and it turns an emergency into a routine. Create the new key beside the old one, move the consumers, verify, wait, delete. Put that on a schedule and the quiet backbone of your BTP integrations stops being its quietest risk.

title: Joule Agents on SAP Cloud ERP Private: What Really Happens When You Try to Activate One
author: VineetBakshi
text:
A customer has AI Units, Business Data Cloud and an approved finance use case. They still cannot switch on a single agent, and the reason is not on any architecture slide. This post walks through how to think about it, what the options actually are, and how to work out 
 which path fits your landscape.

Every Phase. Every Tool. Every Decision. How SAP Has Woven AI Into Transformation

title: Beyond Architecture: Through My Lens on the Multidimensional Architect in the Age of AI
author: anandtigadikar
text:
Architecting Tomorrow: AI, Autonomy & Impact 
 AI is not just changing how we build technology; it is fundamentally redefining how we think, architect, lead, and create business value. The question is no longer whether AI will transform Enterprise Architecture, but how prepared we are to lead that transformation. 
 Having been part of the SAP Multidimensional Architect Program since its inception in 2024, it has been fascinating to witness how the program has evolved over the last three years — mirroring the rapid transformation of technology, business, and the Enterprise Architecture profession. 
 What began as an initiative to broaden the horizons of Enterprise Architects has progressively evolved into a much deeper conversation around AI, autonomous enterprises, intelligent agents, strategic business leadership, and the changing role of architects in shaping the future. 
 In this blog, I share a few key highlights and reflections through my lens from the 2026 program at the SAP Institute for Product and Engineering in San Ramon, focusing on some fundamental questions: 

 How is AI redefining the role of an Enterprise Architect? 

 How do we move beyond traditional architecture practices to become AI-enabled strategic business leaders? 

 How should architects embrace Agentic AI, autonomous capabilities, and intelligent enterprise ecosystems? 

 What new skills, mindsets, and leadership capabilities must architects develop to stay relevant? 

 Most importantly, how can every architect translate AI innovation into meaningful business outcomes? 
 One thing is becoming increasingly clear: The future belongs to architects who can combine technology, business acumen, AI intelligence, and human leadership. 
 The journey from Enterprise Architecture to AI-driven Enterprise Transformation is already underway. The question is - "are we ready to architect that future"?

title: AI Governance and Cost Monitoring with SAP AI Agent Hub and SAP for Me
author: Amit_SAP_UKI
text:
As organisations deploy hundreds or even thousands of AI agents across SAP and non-SAP environments, governance becomes a critical architectural concern. Enterprise Architects must establish visibility, policy enforcement, observability, identity management, and cost controls before agent ecosystems scale beyond operational control. 
 SAP addresses this challenge through two complementary capabilities: 
 SAP AI Agent Hub provides discovery, inventory, governance, observability, verification, and lifecycle management for AI agents, LLMs and MCP servers across heterogeneous landscapes. 
 SAP4ME acts as the operational and activation layer through which SAP-managed AI capabilities and autonomous services can be provisioned and governed within the SAP ecosystem. 
 Together they form the foundation for enterprise-scale AI governance.

title: Automating CERTRULE exception maintenance in S/4HANA for BTP apps
author: VikasSingh2
text: The previous post used CERTRULE for users with several e-mail addresses. Maintaining the exception list was a two step manual job for Basis, a certificate from the Cloud Connector and an import in CERTRULE, and 500 users took more than 20 hours. This post asks whether both steps are essential and whether they can be automated, and ends with a simple BTP app that loads a CSV file in one step through principal propagation.
